blocks.text: Multi-step reasoning in an agent context means sustaining a coherent chain of reasoning across an entire trajectory of real actions, not just a single internal reasoning pass, weaving together planning, tool selection, and reflection, all covered in earlier topics in this module, into one connected whole.

This topic covers how this differs from chain of thought and plan and solve, both covered in an earlier module as purely internal reasoning techniques, maintaining coherence across a long trajectory, recognizing when reasoning goes off track, and the real cost of sustaining a long multi-step agent process.
1. Multi-Step Reasoning Beyond a Single Chain

blocks.alt: Building on memory prompts, multi-step reasoning covers a long agent trajectory

blocks.text: Multi-step reasoning here refers to an agent sustaining coherent reasoning across many actual actions taken over time, not one continuous block of generated text, but a trajectory made up of many separate steps, each informed by the actions and observations that came before it.
2. How This Differs From Chain of Thought and Plan and Solve

blocks.alt: Chain of thought and plan and solve reason internally, multi-step reasoning here interleaves reasoning with real actions

blocks.text: Chain of thought and plan and solve, both covered in an earlier module, reason entirely within generated text toward an answer, agent multi-step reasoning genuinely interleaves reasoning with real actions and their actual results, extending the ReAct pattern, also covered earlier, across a potentially long sequence of steps rather than just one or two.

blocks.text: 3. Interleaving Reasoning With Actions Across Many Steps

blocks.alt: Reason leads to act, then observe, then reason again, act again, and observe again, repeating

blocks.text: Each cycle in a long agent trajectory follows the reason, act, observe pattern from the earlier ReAct topic, but a genuinely multi-step task chains many of these cycles together, with each round reasoning conditioned not just on the original goal but on everything actually observed across every prior cycle.

code.content:
trajectory = []
for step in range(max_steps):
    reasoning = model.generate(build_prompt(goal, trajectory))
    action = parse_action(reasoning)
    observation = execute(action)
    trajectory.append((reasoning, action, observation))
    if is_goal_complete(trajectory):
        break

blocks.text: 4. Maintaining Coherence Across a Long Trajectory

blocks.alt: An early step decision still needs to make sense many steps later

blocks.text: A genuine challenge in multi-step agent reasoning is keeping later steps consistent with decisions made earlier in the same trajectory, a choice made in step two should still make sense in the context of step eight, this connects directly to the memory and context window concerns covered in earlier topics, since the full trajectory history may need to stay accessible for this coherence to hold.
5. When Multi-Step Reasoning Goes Off Track

blocks.alt: A trajectory drifting off course gets caught by reflection

blocks.text: This connects directly back to reflection prompts, covered earlier in this module, a long trajectory can gradually drift away from the original goal without any single step looking obviously wrong on its own, periodic reflection checking overall progress, not just individual step success, is what catches this kind of gradual drift.

blocks.title: Gradual drift is a genuinely different failure mode from a single wrong step
blocks.content: A single clearly wrong action is often easy to catch, a trajectory that drifts slowly, each step reasonable on its own but the overall direction slowly diverging from the goal, is harder to notice without deliberately checking overall progress periodically.

blocks.text: 6. Combining Planning, Tool Selection, and Reflection

blocks.alt: Planning leads to tool selection, then reflection, then back to planning, in a repeating cycle

blocks.text: A genuinely well designed multi-step agent trajectory weaves together every technique covered so far in this module, planning decomposes the goal, tool selection picks the right action for each step, reflection checks whether things are actually going well, and this cycle repeats, adjusting the plan as needed, until the goal is reached.
7. A Worked Multi-Step Agent Trajectory Example

An agent tasked with compiling a competitive analysis report plans an initial sequence of research steps, selects appropriate search and data tools for each, reflects periodically on whether the gathered information genuinely covers the original request, and revises its remaining plan partway through when it discovers, through reflection, that an important competitor was not initially covered.
8. The Real Cost of Long Trajectories

blocks.alt: A long trajectory accumulates real cost and latency

blocks.text: Every additional step in a trajectory, planning, tool execution, reflection, adds its own model calls, cost, and latency, this connects directly to the token and cost optimization concerns covered in an earlier module, a genuinely long trajectory needs to be worth its accumulated cost relative to the value of actually completing the task correctly.
9. Multi-Step Reasoning as a Synthesis

This topic is really where planning, tool selection, routing, memory, and reflection, all covered earlier in this module, come together into one coherent whole, a genuinely capable agent is not any single one of these techniques alone, it is all of them working together across a sustained, coherent multi-step trajectory.
Worked Example

A developer builds a research agent that plans five steps upfront and executes them without any coherence checking along the way, by step four, the agent has drifted from the original narrow research question toward a related but genuinely different topic, none of the individual steps looked obviously wrong when they happened.

Adding a periodic reflection check specifically comparing accumulated progress against the original goal statement, not just checking whether each individual step succeeded, catches this drift by step three instead of only at the very end, allowing the agent to correct course with two steps still remaining rather than needing to discard the entire trajectory.
Common Mistakes

items: Treating each step in a trajectory as independent instead of maintaining coherence with everything decided earlier
Only checking whether individual steps succeeded, missing the gradual drift of an overall trajectory away from the actual goal
Letting a trajectory run indefinitely without weighing its accumulated cost against the value of completing the task
Confusing this agent-level, action-interleaved reasoning with the purely internal chain of thought or plan and solve techniques from an earlier module

blocks.text: Practice

Design a five step agent trajectory for a task you are familiar with, combining planning, tool selection, and at least one reflection checkpoint, and identify specifically at which step reflection should check overall progress against the original goal rather than just individual step success.
Key Takeaway

Multi-step reasoning in an agent context sustains coherent reasoning across a long trajectory of real actions, weaving together planning, tool selection, and reflection into one connected whole, distinct from chain of thought and plan and solve because it interleaves reasoning with genuine actions and their observed results across potentially many steps, at a real accumulated cost worth weighing against the task value.
